source.title: Why Has Predicting Downstream Capabilities of Frontier AI Models with Scale Remained Elusive?
source.authors: Rylan Schaeffer; Hailey Schoelkopf; Brando Miranda; Gabriel Mukobi; Varun Madan; Adam Ibrahim; Herbie Bradley; Stella Biderman; O. Koyejo

record.file_problem: The supplied text is truncated to the first 400000 of 587471 characters; it cuts off within appendix figure material.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how predictable multiple-choice downstream evaluation scores are across scale, and finds that evaluation transformations weaken their relationship with compute. It refines the scope of downstream predictability rather than testing pretraining loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates per-sample multiple-choice scores across model families and compute, and reports outcomes bearing on downstream predictability. It does not fit or test held-out pretraining cross-entropy power laws, small-to-large loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It also reports figure-based per-benchmark distributions in Appendix H; those individual plots are not transcribed as separate rows.
record.test_reason: Across five model families and many multiple-choice benchmarks, the study measures per-sample correlations between scores and pretraining compute. It shows that the correct-choice log-likelihood tracks compute closely, while choices-normalized probability, Brier Score and Accuracy track it progressively less. This bears directly on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6) and argues that the version needs restating for standard MCQA metrics.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the transformations from per-sample correct-choice log-likelihood to pChoices, Brier Score and Accuracy progressively degrade the relationship with compute, because these metrics depend on probability mass on specific incorrect choices. Continuous metrics like Brier Score do not restore predictability. Modeling per-choice incorrect mass might help, but whether it can be fit and extrapolated is left open.
record.recipe_differences: The study computes per-sample score-compute correlations and compares metric transformations; it does not fit or evaluate the original pretraining-loss power-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation metric changes predictability: choices normalization and accuracy reduce score-compute correlations; Brier Score has little-to-no effect on the correlation distribution relative to choices-normalized probability.

fits_no_version.finding: Probability mass on incorrect choices positively covaries with correct-choice mass and typically rises with compute, but at a given correct-choice probability it varies by orders of magnitude.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-sample incorrect-choice probability mass may follow scaling trends, but with large spread, which limits MCQA metric prediction.

record.problems: The study is restricted to log-likelihood-based multiple-choice benchmarks. Its analyses use scores from entire model families across several orders of magnitude and do not employ backtesting; the authors state that predicting change points in advance remains future work. The supplied text is truncated, and Appendix H contains many per-benchmark figure results not individually extracted here.
record.rows_left_out: Per-benchmark and per-model-family figure-only distributions in Appendix H, Figures 10-79, were not extracted separately because the dense panels do not provide textual numerical values that can be reliably assigned to each condition. The text states the patterns are consistent across benchmarks and provides aggregate ordering frequencies in r6-r8.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream scores from pretraining loss; actual extrapolation or backtesting to larger models (the authors state they do not backtest); generative and non-MCQA tasks; aggregate benchmark scores as opposed to per-sample correlations.
Not tested: no held-out pretraining loss power-law fits.
Not tested: no small-to-large extrapolation of loss.
Not tested: no compute-optimal allocation analysis.
Not tested: no other modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: no comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: pVocab(correct) carries little information about pChoices(correct), and pChoices<0.5 carries little information about Accuracy. Brier Score is less variable but still loose. This is the direct evidence for the mechanism behind the V6 limit.
The INCITE family was a slight outlier from the other families, possibly due to benchmark contamination in its pretraining data. This is a family-level condition on the results.

record.verdict_notes: Predictability here means per-sample correlation with compute within a model family, computed over full families spanning orders of magnitude, with no held-out extrapolation. The verdicts therefore concern association with scale, not demonstrated forecasting. The text is truncated within the Appendix H figures; the per-benchmark panels are declared in rows_left_out. The record's version statuses are fine apart from the r4 state fix.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating power-law fits from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their scaling exponents.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.

The study tests predictability of log-likelihood-derived multiple-choice scores against pretraining compute; it does not test other downstream task formats or establish prediction from pretraining loss in general.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and bending of fitted power-law curves.

For V6, the relevant fact is that Brier Score stays degraded relative to correct-choice log-probability: Fig. 3C says it 'minorly decreases' correlations and does not restore predictability. 'Partial' describes V6 better than 'absent'.

relationships.condition: Per-sample correct-choice log-probability (or vocabulary probability) on MCQA benchmarks, across model families
relationships.reason: About 90% of ARC-Challenge samples have score-compute correlation >0.75 regardless of family, and the exp transform leaves rank correlations unchanged (r1, r2). This is correlation with compute, not tested extrapolation.
relationships.display_finding: About 90% of ARC-Challenge samples have score-compute correlations above 0.75 regardless of model family, and exponentiation preserves rank correlations.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Per-sample correct-choice log-probability (or vocabulary probability) on MCQA benchmarks, across model families
source_check.reason: Strong positive score-compute correlations support V6 in this tested setting; exponentiation preserves Spearman and Kendall correlations. Extrapolation is untested.

relationships.condition: Standard MCQA metrics: choices-normalized probability, Brier Score, Accuracy
relationships.reason: Choices normalization cuts the share of samples with correlation >0.75 to 40% (r3). Brier Score does not recover predictability (r4) and Accuracy decorrelates further (r5). The ordering holds in at least 82.4–90.4% of tuples (r6–r8), so predictability depends on the metric choice.
relationships.display_finding: Choice normalization reduced the share of samples with correlation above 0.75 to 40%, Brier score did not restore predictability and accuracy weakened correlations further, with the ordering holding in at least 82.4–90.4% of tuples.

source_check.condition: Standard MCQA metrics: choices-normalized probability, Brier Score, Accuracy
source_check.reason: Choices normalization weakens correlations, Brier Score does not restore them, and accuracy weakens them further. This establishes metric-dependent predictability rather than uniform absence.

relation.reason: The study directly measures relationships between downstream scores and pretraining compute across model families and benchmarks.

tranche.reason: Its results and mechanism qualify downstream predictability by showing that incorporating incorrect-choice probabilities degrades score-compute correlations.

source_check.notes: Correlations are computed per sample within each model family, not from pooled family scores. Appendix B explicitly states that the analyses use entire model families and do not employ backtesting.

statements.correction: ARC-Challenge: approximately 90% of samples have Spearman score-compute correlation >0.75 for correct-choice log vocabulary probability; only 40% after choices normalization; accuracy further decreases correlations. V6 verdict for standard MCQA metrics: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The ARC-Challenge comparison is accurate, but the challenges label overstates this study's metric-dependent, incomplete relationship with scale.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Log-likelihood-derived multiple-choice metrics, especially choices-normalized scores and accuracy
reader_labels.reason: Correct-choice log-probability is strongly correlated with compute, but choices normalization reduces the fraction above 0.75 and accuracy reduces correlations further; Brier Score does not restore the lost predictability (r1-r5). The reported metric ordering holds for most, but not all, tested tuples (r6-r8).
